prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology and bioactive form of glucagon-like peptide-1 that enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: GLP-1 is the one shortlisted candidate with a complete arc from physiology (the incretin effect, proglucagon processing, identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, receptor biology) to a therapeutic class that has changed the care of type 2 diabetes and obesity, with cardiovascular and renal outcome data. Five of six members ranked it first and all six placed it in the top two, so it is the only candidate where support does not depend on a particular taste for method, cell biology or drug development. It is mature, independently confirmed, and the clinical impact is still growing, so recognition is timely. On the attribution question I have moved from my opening trio (Drucker, Holst, Knudsen) to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The prize is for discovery, and Mojsov's identification of the biologically active peptide is a discovery step that the later analogues depended on. Knudsen's work was decisive for the drugs, but it is development of analogues for an already defined target.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Four credited people and an uncredited contributor (Habener) compete for three places, and the priority history of the active-peptide work is contested, so any trio leaves someone with a real claim. A second concern is that the clinical product owes much to industrial development, and a trio of physiologists could be read as overlooking the people who made the therapy work in patients. If the committee wants the prize to reward the translation, my configuration is the weaker one. Finally, a single-achievement prize on a candidate everyone ranks highly could be accused of consensus by default, so I want the scientific case tested rather than assumed.

responses.point: Drucker, Holst and Mojsov are the most defensible discovery trio, and Knudsen's role is engineering of long-acting analogues, so credit boundaries between discovery and development are contestable.
responses.response: I now agree with this and have changed my opening allocation. I had included Knudsen because the acylated analogue is what patients receive. But the Medicine prize has more often honoured the discovery that makes a therapy conceivable. I do not accept that Knudsen's role is only engineering, since a durable, once-weekly peptide required real insight into binding and half-life. The way to credit that is the citation wording about enabling therapies, not a fourth discovery name. I also share your discomfort with leaving Boyden, Bamberg and Miesenboeck out of optogenetics (B044). That allocation problem is worse than the one in GLP-1.

responses.point: Ranked the unfolded protein response (B010, Walter and Mori) first as an original, mechanistically clear and conceptually general discovery with a clean two-person configuration, and proposed Holst, Drucker and Knudsen for GLP-1, noting Mojsov's claim is unresolved.
responses.response: I agree that B010 has the cleanest attribution on the list and a very strong conceptual case. My disagreement is about the Medicine link. The UPR connection to diabetes, neurodegeneration and cancer is indirect, and no therapy has yet come from it, whereas GLP-1 has both the mechanism and the proven benefit. I rank B010 below B016 and below the three candidates I list as alternatives or consider next, but I would not oppose it as a second part. On your trio, I think Knudsen's inclusion ahead of Mojsov puts weight on industrial development over the discovery of the active peptide. I would keep Mojsov, but I accept that this is a judgement call and the committee may split on it.

responses.point: Proposed Hall and Schreiber for TOR, leaving Sabatini out because of public integrity-related controversy, while admitting that omitting mammalian mTOR identification is a weakness.
responses.response: I take the attribution problem seriously, but I would separate it from the scientific case. Hall's yeast genetics is the founding discovery, and the Schreiber FKBP12-rapamycin work is part of the route to the target, so Hall and Schreiber are a coherent pair. I would not give weight to unverified controversy in the record, and the supplied evidence does not let me evaluate it. My concern is the one you raise: a TOR prize that skips the mammalian identification (Brown, Sabers, Sabatini) is scientifically incomplete. This is why I keep B003 as an alternative and not as the preferred configuration. I agree with you on B016 and on Mojsov.

responses.point: Ranked optogenetics second, as a transformative experimental invention that is entering clinical use, while admitting that credit is spread across at least six people, and that medical impact is early compared with its research impact.
responses.response: I accept that optogenetics changed experimental biology, but I place it lower for the reasons you give yourself. With six credited people, any three-name configuration will be disputed, and the clinical evidence is early for a Physiology or Medicine prize. A trio of Deisseroth, Nagel and Hegemann leaves out Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenboeck, who each have a defensible claim. I would prefer a candidate whose allocation can be defended on the evidence. I do agree with your point that Knudsen's role is industrial translation, and that is part of why I changed my allocation.

responses.point: Ranked GLP-1 first with Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, spanning physiology to drug design, and put CAR-T second as a new therapeutic modality with clear clinical proof.
responses.response: I see the logic of a physiology-to-drug-design trio, and it is the best argument against my current allocation. My answer is that the three-person limit forces a choice between discovering the active peptide and developing the analogue, and I would favour the discovery. On CAR-T I agree it is a strong second-tier candidate and I rank it third. My hesitation is that the supplied credit leaves out Eshhar and others with early chimeric receptor claims, so the trio of June, Sadelain and Rosenberg may not map onto the decisive steps.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov or Knudsen should take the third place in the GLP-1 trio, and how much weight the record gives to the Habener-lab contribution and priority history.
Whether a majority of the committee prefers a physiology-based trio or a physiology-to-therapy trio for GLP-1.
Whether a second achievement (for example TOR or CAR-T) would improve the configuration or only complicate the credit, since each adds attribution problems that GLP-1 alone avoids.
How much weight clinical translation should carry against basic discovery for B010 and B009, where therapies are still pending.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My research field is autoimmunity (Sjogren's disease, lupus, Ro52/TRIM21), which is adjacent to cGAS-STING (B009) and CAR-T in autoimmunity, but this is topical overlap and not a personal or institutional connection. Known co-authors (Vijay Kuchroo, Sven-Erik Sonesson) are not credited on any shortlisted candidate, and my Bergen affiliation and the shared KI setting do not establish a tie to any credited person.
